High-Speed Cornering and Pumping Through Turns

Performance outcome

The rider manages entry speed, vision, line, pressure and lean as one connected system, so they exit corners faster and set up for what comes next, in flat turns, berms, off-cambers and linked corners alike.

Who it’s for

Advanced riders and racers who lose time in corners: braking too late or too much, sliding, running wide or sinking back.

Before this lesson

  • Advanced Body Position.
  • Pressure Control.
  • Brake to Go Faster is recommended alongside this lesson.

Why it matters

Most trails are a series of corners joined by straights. Exit speed carries down the next straight, so small gains at the corner exit add up over a whole run. Even elite riders keep working on their cornering.

Technical model

Source check: d09 (could not be opened). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

Corner types ask for different things

Flat turns depend on tyre grip from lean and pressure; berms let the rider push into a supporting wall; off-camber turns slope away and reduce grip; linked turns make one corner the setup for the next. A cue that works in a berm can fail in a flat turn.

Entry speed is set before the corner

Most corners are won or lost at the entry. Speed is best set before the turn, so the rider can release the brakes and let the tyres use their grip for turning.

Vision and line

Looking for the exit early lets the rider choose an entry that suits it. Wide-in, tight-out and early-apex lines trade entry speed against exit speed.

Pressure and lean

Pressure through the outside foot and the bars keeps the tyres loaded; leaning the bike more than the body keeps the rider’s mass over the contact patches. Where the corner shape allows, loading the bike through the turn and releasing on the exit can pump speed out of it.

Linked corners

Between linked corners, staying light out of the first and loading the second (rather than pedalling between them) protects weight and line into the corner that matters most.

Physics & maths

Centripetal force and lean angle

To follow a curve of radius r at speed v, the tyres must supply a sideways force of mv²/r. Grip, roughly the friction coefficient times the normal force, limits how much they can give. Double the speed and the force needed quadruples, which is why entry speed matters so much. For an idealised bike on flat ground, the balanced lean angle θ satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg). A berm tilts the ground and lets part of the normal force do the turning, which is why berms can be taken faster.

An idealised model: real tyres, berms and riders are messier. A good Mathlete visual: a slider for speed and radius showing the required force and lean angle.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Braking into the corner and through it.Entry speed too high; late vision; lack of trust in grip.Coach to supply
Front wheel washes out in flat turns.Too little front pressure, often from sinking back; too much lean or speed for the grip.Coach to supply
Exits wide.Late vision; early apex; too much entry speed.Coach to supply
Sinking back and sitting on the bike mid-corner.Fatigue; fear; position with no range left.Coach to supply
Over-slowing: safe but slow everywhere.Not knowing the available grip; braking at fixed habits rather than for the corner.Coach to supply

Where sources disagree

  • Pedal position in flat turns: sources differ (outside pedal down versus level pedals). The audit recorded this rather than merging it; the coach should decide what to teach and when.

Practice design

Setting
A coach-selected set of corners the rider knows: ideally a flat turn, a berm and a pair of linked turns, at below race pace.
Focus
Change one variable at a time: brake marker, entry line or where the rider looks. Keep the others the same.
Feedback
Film from a safe spot that shows entry, apex and exit; time a short segment through the corner if possible.

Stop when

  • Conditions change (corner blowing out, braking bumps, wet).
  • The rider starts adding speed instead of testing the focus.
  • Fatigue.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Where braking finishes relative to the turn-in.
  • Front-wheel pressure and position mid-corner.
  • Line: entry, apex and exit points.
  • Exit speed (segment time if available).
  • Consistency across several runs.

Ready to move on

  • Coach-observed: consistent entry, line and exit through a known set of corners, with braking finished before turn-in where the corner allows.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
